note: Every entry was checked against its official site on the verified_on date. Site coordinates are approximate (to about 0.1 degree); entries with approx=true give the region only.

entries.name: MicroObservatory
entries.do: Pick an object from a menu, choose a filter and exposure, and a small robotic telescope in Arizona takes the picture for you. You get the image (FITS and GIF) back by email.
entries.wait: Queued for the next clear night; usually back within a day or two
entries.first: Image the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) or the Orion Nebula (M42) through red, green and blue filters, then combine the three into your first color picture.
entries.note: The DIY Planet Search observations are temporarily suspended; ordinary imaging continues.

entries.name: Global Sky Partners
entries.price: Free to students through a partner programme
entries.do: LCO gives over 1,000 hours a year on its robotic telescope network to about 30 education partners, who run supported projects, workshops and mentoring for schools.
entries.wait: Queue-scheduled across the network: hours to a few days
entries.first: Ask your teacher to join a partner such as Comet Chasers or 100 Global High School Teams, then measure the light curve of a variable star.

entries.name: Serol's Cosmic Explorers
entries.do: A game-like series of challenges for ages 8 and up. Each one ends with you requesting a real picture from LCO's 0.4-metre robotic telescopes and earning a badge.
entries.wait: Your picture is queued on the network: usually a few days
entries.first: Sign up (free), complete the first challenge and take your first real image; badges unlock the next missions.

entries.name: Faulkes Telescope Project
entries.operator: Dill Faulkes Educational Trust with LCO
entries.do: School projects on the two 2-metre Faulkes Telescopes (Hawaiʻi and Australia) and LCO's smaller telescopes, with teacher training and ready-made activities.
entries.first: Photograph a comet on two nights and measure how far it moved against the stars.

entries.name: Skynet Robotic Telescope Network
entries.operator: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC)
entries.price: Through a course, Skynet Junior Scholars or a partner institution
entries.do: Queue exposures on about ten optical telescopes worldwide from a web interface and download calibrated FITS images. A next-generation platform (Skynet Global Observatory) is in preview.
entries.first: Image a globular cluster in two filters and plot its color–magnitude diagram.

entries.name: iTelescope
entries.price: Paid plans: prepaid points, charged per imaging hour
entries.do: Rent research-grade telescopes at dark-sky sites, either live or as automated plans, and download the raw and calibrated FITS files.
entries.wait: Real-time sessions; images minutes after each exposure
entries.first: Book one hour on a wide-field telescope and shoot a hydrogen-alpha image of an emission nebula.

entries.name: Telescope Live
entries.price: Paid monthly or yearly plans; yearly student cards
entries.do: Request observations on professional-grade astrographs, or download finished multi-hour datasets from its archive and process them yourself.
entries.wait: Archive data instantly; new requests take days to weeks
entries.first: Download an archive dataset of a galaxy and practice stacking and stretching it before paying for new time.

entries.name: Slooh
entries.do: Reserve telescope time or join shared 'missions', and watch live shows where astronomers talk through what the telescopes are seeing.
entries.wait: Images within minutes of your reserved slot
entries.first: Join a Moon mission and build a mosaic of the terminator, where the craters cast long shadows.

entries.name: PICTOR radio telescope
entries.do: Submit a drift-scan observation from 1300 to 1700 MHz with a 1.5-metre dish in Athens. You choose the center frequency, bandwidth, channels and duration and get plots (plus optional raw data as CSV) by email.
entries.wait: Runs as soon as the dish is free; results minutes after the scan
entries.first: Wait until the Milky Way crosses Athens' zenith (see the live meter in the guide below), then catch the hydrogen line at 1420.4 MHz.

entries.name: Skynet 20-metre radio telescope
entries.operator: Green Bank Observatory and UNC Skynet
entries.price: Through a Skynet course or programme
entries.do: Control a 20-metre dish in West Virginia through the Skynet interface: map radio sources, scan the Sun or record the hydrogen line.
entries.first: Make a radio map of the Sun and compare it with today's ultraviolet image from the Solar Dynamics Observatory.

entries.name: Goldstone Apple Valley Radio Telescope (GAVRT)
entries.operator: Lewis Center for Educational Research with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
entries.do: Trained teachers and their classes remotely operate a 34-metre former Deep Space Network antenna at Goldstone, California, in live science campaigns.
entries.first: Teachers: complete the training, then run a live observing session with your class.

entries.name: Radio JOVE
entries.price: Free to join; the receiver kit is bought separately
entries.do: Build a simple shortwave radio telescope (around 20 MHz) that hears radio storms from Jupiter and the Sun, and share or listen to recordings from stations worldwide.
entries.wait: Instant for archive recordings; your own station depends on Jupiter's geometry
entries.first: Listen to archived Jupiter storms first, then predict the next one visible from where you live.

entries.name: Solar observatory (this site)
entries.do: Today's real Sun from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) and GOES weather satellites, side by side.
entries.first: Find today's biggest sunspot group, then look for it again tomorrow to watch the Sun rotate.

entries.name: SDO: The Sun Now
entries.do: The latest images from all nine ultraviolet channels of the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) plus magnetograms, at up to 4096 pixels, each with a 48-hour movie.
entries.first: Compare the 171 Å and 304 Å images: find a loop system over an active region in one and its footprint in the other.

entries.name: SOHO: the very latest images
entries.do: Real-time coronagraph images (LASCO C2 and C3) that block the Sun's disk to reveal its outer atmosphere, plus extreme-ultraviolet images.
entries.first: Watch the LASCO C3 movie for a coronal mass ejection (CME) leaving the Sun.

entries.name: Helioviewer
entries.do: Browse decades of solar images from many spacecraft, layer wavelengths and make your own time-lapse movies of any date.
entries.first: Make a one-day movie of the Sun on your birthday.

entries.name: Virtual Telescope Project WebTV
entries.do: Free live broadcasts from robotic telescopes in Italy: close-approaching asteroids, comets, eclipses and planetary events, with commentary.
entries.first: Catch the next near-Earth asteroid flyby live and watch it move against the stars.

entries.name: ESO observatory webcams
entries.do: Round-the-clock webcams at ESO's sites in the Atacama Desert, including Paranal (the Very Large Telescope) and La Silla.
entries.first: Watch the Very Large Telescope (VLT) domes open at sunset. The map on this page shows when it is dark there.

entries.name: Extremely Large Telescope construction webcams
entries.do: Watch the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), set to be the world's largest optical telescope, being built on Cerro Armazones.
entries.first: Take a screenshot each month and make a time-lapse of the dome closing over the telescope.

entries.name: Maunakea summit webcams
entries.do: Live views of the domes on Maunakea, 4,200 metres up, including all-sky cameras that show stars and clouds at night.
entries.first: Check the all-sky camera at night and identify the Milky Way and bright planets.

entries.name: Live views from the International Space Station
entries.do: NASA's official stream of high-definition views of Earth from the International Space Station (ISS), when the cameras and link are available.
entries.wait: Live (gaps when the station is out of contact)
entries.first: Watch an orbital sunrise: the ISS sees one about every 90 minutes.

entries.name: NASA Live
entries.do: Every live NASA broadcast in one place: launches, spacewalks, landings and briefings.
entries.first: Watch the next launch with the Rocket hangar page open beside it to compare the vehicle.

entries.name: Stellarium Web
entries.do: A full planetarium in your browser: tonight's sky for your location, over a billion stars from Gaia, deep-sky objects, planets and satellites, at any date and time.
entries.first: Find where the Andromeda Galaxy will be at 9 pm tonight, then go outside and look (see the guide below).

entries.name: WorldWide Telescope
entries.do: Pan and zoom across all-sky surveys in many wavelengths, overlay images from Hubble and Webb, and play guided tours.
entries.first: Compare the Orion Nebula in visible light and infrared, then play a guided tour.

entries.name: ESASky
entries.do: Explore the whole sky from gamma rays to radio waves, see the footprints of Hubble, Webb, XMM-Newton and Gaia observations of any target, and download the data.
entries.first: Search for the Crab Nebula (M1) and switch from X-ray to radio to watch the supernova remnant change shape.

entries.name: Aladin Lite
entries.operator: Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg (CDS)
entries.do: A lightweight sky atlas of hundreds of surveys (Hierarchical Progressive Surveys, HiPS) with catalogue overlays. Our Sky surveys page embeds it.
entries.first: Overlay the Gaia catalogue on the Pleiades and see the cluster members' shared motion.

entries.name: NASA's Eyes on the Solar System
entries.do: A 3D solar system with every NASA spacecraft where it really is, plus replays of key mission events.

links.label: Replay the New Horizons Pluto flyby

entries.first: Replay New Horizons' 2015 Pluto flyby and follow the spacecraft's camera.

entries.name: NASA's Eyes on Asteroids
entries.do: Every known near-Earth asteroid and comet in 3D, with upcoming close approaches and the spacecraft that visit them.
entries.first: Find the next five close approaches and check how close each one comes compared with the Moon.

entries.name: NASA's Eyes on the Earth
entries.do: Earth-observing satellites in their real orbits, with recent data layers such as temperature, carbon dioxide and sea level.
entries.first: Follow one satellite for an orbit and see which data set it measures.

entries.name: NASA's Eyes on Exoplanets
entries.do: Fly to thousands of confirmed exoplanet systems and see artist models built from real measurements.
entries.first: Visit TRAPPIST-1 and compare its seven planets' orbits with Mercury's.

entries.name: Deep Space Network (DSN) Now
entries.do: Which spacecraft each giant Deep Space Network dish is talking to right now, with signal strength and round-trip light time.
entries.first: Find Voyager 1 on a dish and note its round-trip light time: that is the delay for every command sent to it.

entries.name: NASA's Eyes on Mars 2020
entries.do: Follow the Perseverance rover and Ingenuity helicopter across Jezero Crater and replay the landing.
entries.first: Replay the landing here, then fly it yourself on our Mars landing page.

entries.name: Stellarium (desktop)
entries.do: The full desktop planetarium: huge star catalogues, realistic skies, eclipse simulation and a plug-in that can steer a real telescope on a computerized mount.
entries.first: Simulate the next total solar eclipse from the center line and time totality.

entries.name: Gaia Sky
entries.do: Fly through the Milky Way in 3D using real Gaia positions for over a billion stars, with virtual reality support.
entries.first: Leave the solar system and look back: watch the constellations distort as you move.

entries.name: OpenSpace
entries.operator: American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), Linköping University and partners
entries.do: The planetarium-dome software used by museums: the known universe from Earth's surface to the cosmic microwave background, with mission replays.
entries.first: Replay a spacecraft flyby, then zoom out to the scale of the observable universe.

entries.name: Celestia
entries.do: A classic real-time 3D space simulator: travel anywhere, change time and follow spacecraft trajectories.
entries.first: Go to Saturn and speed time up to watch the moons' orbits.

entries.name: SpaceEngine
entries.do: A photorealistic universe simulator that mixes real catalogues with procedurally generated galaxies, stars and planets.
entries.first: Visit a real star catalogue entry, then a procedural one, and look for the difference in the info panel.

entries.name: Universe Sandbox
entries.do: A gravity sandbox: collide planets, add a star to the solar system or change the Moon's mass and watch what happens.
entries.first: Double the Sun's mass and watch what happens to Earth's orbit.

entries.name: Kerbal Space Program
entries.do: Design rockets from parts and fly them with real orbital mechanics: orbits, rendezvous, landings and interplanetary transfers.
entries.first: Reach orbit, then do a Hohmann transfer to the Mun. Our Orbit Lab page explains the maths.

entries.name: Orbiter 2024
entries.do: A realistic Newtonian spaceflight simulator for Windows: fly the Space Shuttle or Apollo add-ons, dock with the ISS and plan transfers.
entries.first: Launch the Delta-glider to orbit and dock with the ISS using the built-in autopilots as a guide.

entries.name: JPL Horizons
entries.operator: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory Solar System Dynamics
entries.do: Precise positions of over a million solar system bodies and spacecraft for any time and any place on Earth: the same ephemerides mission planners use.
entries.first: Get Mars' position from your city for tonight, then check it in Stellarium Web.

entries.name: NASA Exoplanet Archive
entries.do: Every confirmed exoplanet with its measured parameters, light curves and transit predictions, with plotting and download tools.
entries.first: Plot planet radius against orbital period for all confirmed planets and find the 'radius valley'.

entries.name: Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST)
entries.do: Download the real data from the Hubble, Webb, TESS and Kepler telescopes once the exclusive-access period ends.
entries.first: Download a Webb image of a galaxy you know and open the FITS file yourself.

entries.name: Minor Planet Center
entries.operator: International Astronomical Union (IAU), hosted at the CfA
entries.do: The official clearinghouse for asteroid and comet positions: look up any object's orbit and observations, or report your own measurements.
entries.first: Look up an asteroid discovered this year and see how many observations its orbit is built from.

entries.name: SDSS SkyServer
entries.do: Images and spectra of millions of galaxies, stars and quasars, with a navigator, school projects and SQL database access.
entries.first: Find a quasar spectrum and measure its redshift from the shifted hydrogen lines.

entries.name: Gaia Archive
entries.do: Positions, distances, motions and colors for nearly two billion stars from ESA's Gaia mission, searchable with ADQL (Astronomical Data Query Language).
entries.first: Pull all stars within 100 parsecs and draw your own Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.

entries.name: Galaxy Zoo
entries.do: Classify galaxy shapes (spirals, bars, mergers) from real survey images; your answers train and check machine classifiers.
entries.first: Classify 20 galaxies and use the 'Talk' board to ask about anything odd you see.

entries.name: Backyard Worlds: Cool Neighbors
entries.do: Blink infrared images to find faint, cold objects such as brown dwarfs close to the Sun.
entries.first: Do the tutorial, then flag your first candidate moving object.

entries.name: Active Asteroids
entries.do: Look at telescope images of asteroids and flag the rare ones showing a tail or coma, like a comet.
entries.first: Classify 50 images: most are ordinary points of light, which makes the tailed ones stand out.

entries.name: Solar Radio Burst Tracker
entries.do: Trace radio bursts from the Sun in dynamic spectra (frequency against time), the radio signature of shocks and energetic electrons.
entries.first: Learn the burst types in the field guide, then mark ten bursts.

entries.name: Rubin Comet Catchers
entries.do: Inspect Vera C. Rubin Observatory images of solar system bodies and spot comet-like activity.
entries.first: Work through the tutorial, then classify your first set of Rubin cutouts.

entries.name: Cloudspotting on Mars
entries.do: Mark the arch-shaped signatures of clouds in data from a Mars orbiter to map when and where Martian clouds form.
entries.first: Mark the arches in ten images, then read the project's results page.

entries.name: Kilonova Seekers
entries.operator: Zooniverse with the Gravitational-wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO)
entries.do: Vet brand-new transients from the GOTO telescopes in near real time; volunteers have co-discovered supernovae and other explosions.
entries.wait: Start in a minute; new images arrive nightly
entries.first: Classify new detections right after a clear night, when fresh transients are waiting.

entries.name: Exoplanet Watch
entries.do: Measure exoplanet transits with the free EXOTIC software, using your own telescope or data requested from a robotic telescope, and upload results to the AAVSO Exoplanet Database.
entries.wait: Minutes for archived data; your own data depends on transit times
entries.first: Reduce a sample data set with EXOTIC and get your first transit light curve.

entries.name: American Association of Variable Star Observers (AAVSO)
entries.price: Free data and guides; optional paid membership
entries.do: Submit brightness estimates of variable stars to a database astronomers have used for over a century, and download light curves of any star.
entries.wait: Instant (data); observing whenever it is clear
entries.first: Plot the light curve of Mira, then estimate its brightness yourself when it is visible.

entries.name: International Astronomical Search Collaboration (IASC)
entries.do: Student teams get fresh survey images from professional telescopes, search them for moving objects and report asteroid detections; confirmed ones can become official discoveries.
entries.first: Form a team with your teacher and sign up for the next Asteroid Search Campaign.
